content: Unscored tablets should not be used because the uniform distribution of the active drug cannot be guaranteed in tablet fragments. Certain tablets, such as heat-stable LPV/r or ATV/r tablets, are manufactured using a specialized embedded matrix formulation (a proprietary melt extrusion technology that stabilizes heat-labile drug molecules). These tablets must not be cut, split, dissolved, chewed, or crushed, as doing so significantly reduces their bioavailability. They should always be swallowed whole. For children requiring an LPV/r-based regimen, LPV/r is available in a 40 mg/10 mg pellet or granule formulation for infants and young children. However, children weighing 10 kg or more should transition to heat-stable LPV/r tablets as soon as they can swallow tablets whole. This transition improves administration, enhances palatability, and reduces pill burden. After the first four weeks of life, infants and children should be weighed at each clinical visit, and their medication doses should be adjusted based on observed growth and changes in body weight. National programs should consider the regulatory and local availability status of specific dosage forms when developing treatment recommendations for children. Ongoing research is being conducted to establish dosing guidance for neonates, infants, and young children for several antiretroviral (ARV) medications. Age indications for each drug are based on current evidence and will be updated as new recommendations become available. For infants at least four weeks old but weighing less than 3 kg, the immaturity of renal and hepatic elimination pathways is less concerning, but uncertainty remains regarding appropriate ARV dosing for preterm and low-birth-weight infants. Doses for this age group are reduced to account for their decreased ability to excrete and metabolize medications. The LPV/r liquid formulation requires a cold chain for transport and storage. Heat-stable LPV/r tablets must be swallowed whole and should not be split, chewed, dissolved, or crushed. Adult 200/50 mg LPV/r tablets can be used for children weighing 14–<25 kg (one tablet in the morning and one in the evening) and for children weighing 25–<35 kg (two tablets in the morning and one in the evening). LPV/r pellets should not be used for infants younger than three months. More details on administering LPV/r pellets are available. The LPV/r granule formulation is approved for use from two weeks of age, but its use in neonates weighing 2–3 kg is based on limited clinical data and substantial uncertainty. If no other formulation exists, one sachet twice daily may be considered for neonates older than two weeks and weighing 2–3 kg to minimize the risk of potential toxicity from overdosing. RAL granules for oral suspension are approved for newborns weighing at least 2 kg. These should be administered once daily during the first week of life and twice daily thereafter. The feasibility and acceptability of RAL granules in resource-limited settings have been demonstrated, provided adequate training and counseling are available. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved simplified dosing of DTG 50 mg film-coated tablets for all children weighing ≥20 kg. However, DTG dispersible tablets and film-coated tablets are not bioequivalent; 30 mg of DTG dispersible tablets corresponds to 50 mg of DTG film-coated tablets. DTG 50 mg film-coated tablets are preferred for children weighing ≥20 kg unless they cannot swallow tablets. Safety monitoring remains important due to limited experience with this dosing. For adolescents living with HIV and weighing more than 30 kg, a fixed-dose formulation of TDF 300 mg, 3TC 300 mg, and DTG 50 mg (TLD) is preferred. During periods of transition or in special circumstances (e.g., neonatal treatment, TB co-treatment, and third-line ART), dosage forms included in the ARV Limited-use Formulary are sufficient to provide appropriate dosing across weight bands for children. The need for new formulations remains critical. Efforts are ongoing to develop better age-appropriate formulations for infants and children living with HIV. For example, a solid fixed-dose combination formulation (ABC/3TC/LPV/r granules) is in the final stages of approval. Additionally, the availability of co-formulated DRV/r in a heat-stable fixed-dose combination is essential to facilitate treatment sequencing and uptake of future secondand third-line regimens for children. WHO continues to work toward simplifying prescribing, dispensing, and dosing guidance for children and adolescents while collaborating with the pharmaceutical industry to optimize drug formulations.
